2주 The WSJ is reporting on a looming debt wall for private equity backed companies. According to the article, PE funds are using cash from new funds to invest preferred equity as a sweetener to get lenders to agree to maturity extensions. For founders with rollover equity, this will dilute your return upon exit. Check the constituent documents, including any stockholders' agreement, for any veto or consent rights. For prospective rollover founders, be aware of this risk. It is a question of degree, but preferred equity could wipe out any return to the common holders in an exit scenario, similar to participating preferred in a VC deal. "[PE fund], which had just raised a $15 billion fund, gave the [portfolio company] $175 million in exchange for preferred shares. Lenders extended due dates for the debt to 2030 and 2031, made an additional loan of roughly $100 million and agreed that [portfolio company] could defer some interest payments. 3주 Can a 0.61% difference cost you ₹7.53 lakh? While analysing mutual funds, I explored how expense ratios can impact long-term wealth creation. I compared the Regular and Direct Growth plans of Parag Parikh Flexi Cap Fund. Both share the same fund manager and underlying portfolio, but differ in expense ratio due to the distribution structure. Regular Plan: 1.30% Direct Plan: 0.69% On an illustrative ₹10 lakh investment, this difference translates to ₹7.53 lakh over 13 years. The takeaway? Compounding works both ways. It can help grow your wealth, but recurring costs can quietly work against it.
